title: Mobile Cobot Safety Validation Lab
one_liner: A van-based lab that measures collision forces and signs off robot and cobot cells against the 2025 ISO 10218 revisions.
customer: Cobot distributors, integrators and 10-200 person manufacturers deploying cells. EHS managers and insurers are the second buyers.
problem: North American robot orders are broadening into semiconductors, pharma and food, and cobots are 15.4% of units. The 2025 revisions of ISO 10218-1 and -2 (which absorbed the collaborative guidance of ISO/TS 15066) require documented risk assessment and validation. Few engineers can do it, and force-measurement gear costs tens of thousands of dollars. Distributors skip validation and the liability lands on the shop and its insurer.
solution: A van with a calibrated force and pressure measurement device, safety-scanner zone tester and stop-time tester. Technicians validate on site (contact-force mapping by body region, speed and separation checks) and deliver a signed report. Software stores and versions results for audits. Annual revalidation is a subscription.
why_now: Revised standards are in force, robot demand is broadening to small shops and new sectors, and mobile manipulators are coming into plants.
revenue_model: $2.5-6k per cell validation. White-label contracts with distributors. About $1.2k a year for revalidation. Referral fees from insurers.
non_obvious_insight: The limiting step for small-shop robots is fear of liability, not price. A third-party validation stamp is what insurers and owners want, and distributors have the incentive to sell but not the independence or equipment to certify.
first_30_days: Rent or buy a used force-measurement device. Sign three cobot distributors. Complete a machinery functional-safety credential. Validate the first five cells at a discount.

title: Human Failover Retainer for Agent-Run Businesses
one_liner: Backup-generator economics for know-how: a retained, drilled bench of human operators that takes over within hours when a company's AI agents fail.
customer: Owners and COOs of 10-200 person companies that replaced back-office headcount with AI agents. First niche: freight brokerages (dispatch, carrier onboarding, load booking). Then medical billing firms, property managers, insurance agencies and 3PLs.
problem: After automation, the people who knew the manual process leave. Then a model deprecation, provider outage, prompt regression, API key ban or payment-processor freeze halts revenue, and nobody remembers how to do the job by hand. Cloud disaster-recovery plans protect servers, not the tacit process knowledge. That skill decays every month the automation succeeds.
solution: A $1.5-6k/month retainer. Phase 1: shadow the process while it still lives in staff heads and write executable runbooks and checklists. Phase 2: keep a pre-vetted bench of remote operators (ex-dispatchers, ex-billers) who sample live work weekly, so they stay current. Phase 3: run quarterly 'lights-out drills' that switch the agents off for four hours and measure time to recover. Guarantee takeover within two hours, billed hourly on activation. The bench's weekly sampling doubles as gold-label QA that flags agent drift, so the retainer also improves the agents.
why_now: 2025-26 brought large cloud and LLM-API outages (for example the October 2025 AWS us-east-1 incident), fast model deprecation cycles, and boards booking headcount cuts on the strength of agents. Insurers are starting to ask about AI-related business-interruption exposure, which gives a compliance reason to buy.
revenue_model: Monthly retainer tiered by process criticality; activation fees at $60-120 per operator-hour; drill and runbook-documentation fees; an insurer or broker referral channel that offers premium credits for a documented failover plan.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody buys a generator until the blackout, but unlike a generator the failover gets more expensive the more successful the AI rollout is, because human know-how atrophies. The best time to sell is right after a company celebrates automation savings, and the CFO can fund the retainer out of those savings. It is a services business that looks like insurance, with recurring revenue, and a bench of a few dozen part-timers can cover many clients.
first_30_days: Pick freight brokerage and find 40 brokers advertising AI dispatch or quoting. Offer a free two-hour 'lights-out drill' to about 10 of them: switch off the agents, time the recovery and hand back a one-page automation-debt score. Recruit 6 part-time ex-dispatchers as the bench. Convert 3 drill participants to $1.5-2.5k/month retainers. Package the outputs as a case study.

title: Human Trust-Anchor Service for Driverless Freight Hubs
angle: Pairing 2: Logistics and physical automation x Trust and verification markets (lens: witness, inspection and proof of condition)
one_liner: A neutral crew and signature service at autonomous-truck terminals that replaces the driver's role as freight's witness: pre-trip inspection, condition-of-freight capture, signed digital BOL and inspector liaison, priced per handoff.
customer: Autonomous trucking carriers, the shippers, 3PLs and brokers tendering freight to them, and cargo insurers. The first buyer is a claims-sensitive shipper or a broker like Werner's CIO who says 'we have a gap'.
problem: The driver signs the BOL, counts pieces, notes damage, checks the seal and talks to the inspector. Driverless trucks remove that witness. The CVSA enhanced-inspection clearance lasts 24 hours and requires a trained inspector. PrePass/Kodiak bypass covers 581 sites but is live only in Texas and Louisiana. Paper BOLs delay cash about 60 days and cause six-figure invoice disputes. Hub-to-hub autonomy leaves 'hundreds of dollars' of human transfer cost per handoff. Insurers price AV trucks above human ones purely on the unknown.
solution: A per-departure witness desk at transfer hubs and terminals, staffed by trained ex-drivers and ex-inspectors with capture tools. It runs the pre-trip enhanced-inspection checklist and logs the 24-hour clearance. It captures condition of freight (piece count, seal number, photos, weight, temperature, damage detection) and issues a neutral third-party-signed eBOL that shipper, carrier and insurer accept. It also acts as the roadside and first-responder liaison, and packages claims evidence.
why_now: Aurora exits 2026 with about 200 driverless trucks and targets 30,000 by 2030. Gatik reports 85k driverless orders. California's driverless-truck rules took effect Apr 28, 2026 and the Teamsters sued on Aug 5. NHTSA sent a first-responder letter on Jul 8, 2026. Insurers expect AV truck pricing to fall 15-25% a year, so evidence of loads and conditions moves pricing.
revenue_model: $35-$90 per handoff or departure, well under the current human transfer cost. $4k-$8k/mo per hub as a base fee. Insurer-paid discounts and data license. Claims-evidence packages at $150-$400 per incident.
non_obvious_insight: Driverless trucking is sold as removing labor, but what it actually removes is a witness, and freight claims, inspections and insurance pricing all ran on that witness. Whoever re-supplies trusted witness capacity at transfer hubs becomes a required, neutral node. Because the same crew and signature service serve every AV carrier, no competing carrier will build it.
first_30_days: Pick one Texas corridor and one terminal. Recruit 2-3 ex-inspectors or ex-drivers. Offer a shipper's claims team or a broker a free pilot on 20 AV loads, then $60 per handoff. Sign a cargo insurer as design partner to co-develop the claims-evidence package.

title: Investor-Cap Look-Through Checks for Title Companies
one_liner: An API that traces a buyer's LLC web to its parent and counts the homes it controls, so title and escrow can clear the ROAD Act's 350-home limit at closing.
customer: Title and escrow companies, closing attorneys and lenders in single-family-heavy metros. Secondary: mid-size investors (100-349 homes) who need to stay under the cap and prove it.
problem: The ROAD Act bars investors with more than 350 homes from buying existing houses. Compliance depends on affiliate holdings scattered across thousands of LLCs, which the closing agent cannot see. Large buyers will restructure into fragments, and mid-size investors suddenly need to manage headroom. Who is liable when a closing clears wrongly is unresolved.
solution: Entity resolution across county deed records, Secretary of State filings, registered-agent and address graphs and mailing addresses. It returns a portfolio count with a confidence score in seconds, an audit-ready evidence file for the closing, and a headroom dashboard for investors near the cap. Verify statute text, effective date, affiliate definition and exemptions first.
why_now: The law took effect in July 2026, and implementation questions are open now. Title agents are the natural chokepoint, as they already collect ownership details on entity purchases. Entity-resolution tooling and cheaper county record access make a small-team build feasible.
revenue_model: $15-40 per buyer-entity check. $500-2,000 per month SaaS for investors. Enterprise licenses to title underwriters.
non_obvious_insight: The people obligated to comply cannot compute the answer, and the people who can compute it are not in the transaction. The closing desk becomes the enforcement point, and mid-size investors treat their 350th home as a scarce budget, creating a second buyer for the same data.
first_30_days: Build for three metros where large single-family operators concentrate. Ingest deed and Secretary of State data. Sell paid pilots to 5 title agencies and 2 underwriters. Publish a free entity-count explainer to attract inbound.

title: Size-Glide: Reversible Tailoring for GLP-1 Wardrobes
one_liner: Prepaid mail-in take-in tailoring, done with reversible seams, that follows a GLP-1 patient down (and back up) through 3-5 sizes, sold as a retention perk to the telehealth programs that prescribe the drugs.
customer: Two payers. (1) Consumers in months 3-18 of GLP-1 treatment, mostly women 35-60 with a professional wardrobe worth $2-5k. (2) GLP-1 telehealth and employer weight-management programs, who pay a per-member fee because churn is their biggest cost.
problem: Patients drop 2-5 sizes in a year. Buying a new wardrobe at each stage costs $1-3k. Local tailors are slow, inconsistent and expensive, and permanent take-ins ruin a garment when weight comes back. Roughly half of users stop within a year and most regain, so the wardrobe problem repeats in both directions. Programs also lack a tangible, celebratory milestone reward that keeps people enrolled.
solution: A prepaid alteration bag ships to your door. A vetted network of micro-tailors runs a standardized 12-garment menu (waist, hem, darts, sleeves) using reversible methods: basted or removable seams and preserved allowances. Every garment gets a QR tag and a digital 'garment passport' recording each alteration and its size band. Weight milestones trigger reminders ('you are down 15 lb, send the blazers'). A let-out service and a resale or donate-out handoff handle regain and garments that are now too big. Telehealth partners can offer 'your first three take-ins are free' as a milestone reward.
why_now: The Wegovy pill launched in January 2026 and Lilly's oral drug is rolling out this year. GLP-1 households now command roughly $660B in spending power (Numerator, August 2026). Employer coverage and cost pressure are creating start-stop cycles, which makes reversible work the safer product.
revenue_model: Prepaid alteration packs of $250-600 per stage, or a $39-79/month wardrobe plan. B2B2C: $10-25 per member per month from telehealth and employer programs as a retention benefit. Small margin on resale handoffs.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is not clothing, it is tailor turnaround and the trust that a garment can come back to its old size. Reversibility is the moat because regain is the norm, not the exception. The best paying customer is the telehealth company's churn budget, not the patient.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 alteration shops in one metro and write a 12-item price menu. Post in r/Zepbound and r/Ozempic communities and local GLP-1 clinic groups to sell 50 prepaid packs. Run a pilot with one small GLP-1 clinic or telehealth startup using free milestone take-ins. Use QR tags and a spreadsheet for the garment passport, and courier pickup for logistics.

title: Age-Signal Rules Engine for App Developers
one_liner: A 'feature-flag service for minors' law': an SDK that takes the OS or app-store age bracket plus jurisdiction and returns the legally required feature set, with citations and an audit trail.
customer: Mid-size consumer apps, games and edtech (10-500 staff) with under-18 users, their general counsel, and app agencies. Series A-C startups first.
problem: Texas app-store age verification (June 2026), Ohio consent (June 2026), Florida under-14 ban, California's OS age-attestation law, the UK regime, and bans in Australia, Brazil, Indonesia and Malaysia each define brackets and required behavior differently. Engineers hard-code rules and rules change monthly. Fines are large.
solution: A versioned policy graph maintained by lawyers plus LLM change tracking. The SDK returns flags for chat, DMs, push timing, ads, purchases and recommendation feeds per bracket and jurisdiction. It integrates with OS age-range signals and third-party verifiers and logs which rule applied when, for regulators.
why_now: For the first time OS and app stores hand developers an age signal (California signed Oct 2025; Apple and Google age-range APIs, from memory), but nobody says what to do with it. The 'policy ratchet' means fragmentation will grow.
revenue_model: $500-5k a month by MAU tier, plus one-time compliance-matrix audits at $3-6k.
non_obvious_insight: Age-verification vendors sell the signal, and nobody sells the decision: the legal mapping from signal to product behavior. That mapping is the durable moat because laws keep diverging.
first_30_days: Publish a public 8-jurisdiction by 5-feature matrix. Run a newsletter around it. Sell 5 compliance-matrix audits at $4k to game and app teams. Wrap the logic into an SDK by month 3.

title: Ticket Escrow Bot for Fan Communities
angle: Pairing 2: Gaming, entertainment, live experiences, fandoms x Cybersecurity, deepfake fraud, identity verification, scams targeting consumers and businesses
one_liner: A payment-escrow bot for the Discord, WhatsApp and Facebook groups where fans already swap tickets, releasing money only when a cryptographically verifiable ticket-transfer email arrives.
customer: Fans aged 18-35 (K-pop, pop tours, esports, festivals, football supporters) trading tickets peer-to-peer, and the community admins and moderators who police scams manually. Fans pay the fee, and admins get a revenue share.
problem: Ticket fraud thrives in fan groups because the only 'proof' is a screenshot, and generative AI now forges tickets, receipts and transfer confirmations trivially. Official resale is distrusted: per the briefing, Oasis tickets went from GBP 135 to 350+ under dynamic pricing, StubHub's World Cup 2026 tickets failed to reach buyers with class actions following, and the UK CMA ordered StubHub to refund 50,000+ customers over drip pricing. Fans therefore keep swapping in groups, where scammers pretend to transfer tickets or sell the same ticket several times.
solution: The buyer pays into escrow. The seller performs the official transfer in the ticketing app (Ticketmaster, AXS, Eventim, Fever and similar). The buyer sends the platform's 'tickets received' email to a unique escrow address, either forwarded as an .eml attachment or through a narrowly scoped read-only mailbox filter for that sender only. The system validates the DKIM/ARC signature, sender domain, event, section and seat lines, and that the recipient is the buyer, then releases funds after a hold for barcode rotation. Extras: automatic enforcement of a group's face-value cap, light seller verification above thresholds, an admin-facing reputation ledger, and cancellation refunds through an insurance partner. Payments run through a licensed platform-payments partner rather than holding funds directly.
why_now: AI-forged screenshots have made image evidence worthless. Per the briefing, Live Nation lost a federal jury verdict on monopolization in April 2026 and resale fees are under fire, the FTC's all-in pricing rule took effect in May 2025, and StubHub's delivery failures have left fans without a trusted route. Ticketing platforms increasingly move tickets by wallet transfer, so signed transfer emails are now standard.
revenue_model: 4-6% fee on escrowed amount, split between buyer and seller, with 0.5-1% shared with community admins. Premium 'insured swap' add-on. B2B API for promoters that want a safe official fan-swap channel.
non_obvious_insight: You do not need to beat Ticketmaster or become a marketplace. Every major ticketing platform already emits a DKIM-signed transfer email that is very hard to fake, a cheap trust anchor no fan-group scammer can produce. The distribution channel is community admins, who already do unpaid trust-and-safety work and will adopt anything that reduces their scam reports.
first_30_days: Pick one fandom with a high-volume swap group (a K-pop tour or a football supporters' group). Run concierge escrow by hand with a payments-platform account and a script that checks .eml DKIM. Handle 100 swaps at 5% and publish 'scams avoided' stats. Onboard 10 admin partners with a revenue share. Check ticketing terms of service per market before scaling.

title: Driver's Ed for Smartphones, Sold to Parent Groups
angle: Pairing 2: Mental health, loneliness and community x Parenting, childcare deserts and kids/AI/screens
one_liner: Ten-week, cohort-based 'phone license' programs where a whole grade's parents and kids pledge together, kids earn tiered device access through in-person challenges, and the finish is a coming-of-age ceremony.
customer: Parent groups for one grade at one school (PTA/PTO, church youth groups, scout troops, neighborhoods) with kids aged 9-13 facing the first-smartphone decision. Parents pay about $249 per child. PTAs get a rev-share. Later: device partners and employers offering parent benefits.
problem: The first smartphone is a collective-action problem ('everyone else has one'). Parental-control software fails technically (7 in 10 Australian under-16s reportedly still hold accounts) and socially. The first phone has become an unguided adolescent initiation with no ritual, no community and no meaning, while loneliness among the young is rising.
solution: 1) A Parent Pact night to agree shared rules. 2) Ten weekly 90-minute kid sessions with trained youth facilitators covering boredom, friendship, spotting manipulative design, AI-companion literacy and group-chat etiquette, with badges earned in person. 3) Tiered device 'licenses': none, then dumbphone or watch, then a filtered smartphone using OS-level age signals, then full access, each unlocked at cohort milestones with parent sign-off. 4) A License Ceremony with families. 5) An alumni circle with monthly meetups and a parent forum.
why_now: Under-16 bans (Australia Dec 2025, Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Florida) and app-store or OS-level age-assurance laws (California's Digital Age Assurance Act, Texas) are tiering the internet by age. Roblox now tiers by age (Kids, Select, standard). Support for Australia's ban has fallen to 57% and enforcement is leaky, so parents need a home-side complement. Twelve US states have school phone bans.
revenue_model: About $249 per child per cohort, a 15% rev-share to PTAs, bounties on tier-appropriate device or plan activations (verify what partners will pay), a $600 facilitator certification for teachers and youth workers, and later employer-paid parent benefits.
non_obvious_insight: The first smartphone fails as a family decision but works as a class decision. Because the product synchronizes a social graph, its moat is the cohort, not code. And a secular rite of passage supplies the 'meaning' that makes kids willing, which content-filtering apps cannot provide.
first_30_days: Pilot with two elementary schools' 4th- and 5th-grade parent groups through PTA presidents and 'Wait Until 8th' pledge lists. Recruit four facilitators (education or psychology students and retired coaches). Charge $249, run cohorts October-December so graduation lands before holiday phone gifting, and track how many kids stay phone-free until 13.

title: Play Yards: Phone-Free Adventure Clubs for Tweens
one_liner: Membership 'junk playground' clubs staffed by trained playworkers for ages 9-14 (tools, timber, fire pits, no phones, no lessons), launched first in four-day-school-week districts where Friday is a childcare hole.
customer: Parents of 9-14-year-olds paying $150-250/month for after-school access or $45-60 per full Friday, plus landlords with vacant retail or barns. Some state child-care subsidies and school-choice funds may help later.
problem: Schools are banning phones and governments are restricting youth social media, but kids have nowhere to go for unstructured, semi-supervised time with peers. Structured enrichment (coding camps, leagues) is oversupplied, while true adventure playgrounds are rare, nonprofit and mostly for younger children.
solution: A leased warehouse, church hall or barn plus a yard, stocked with loose parts, real tools and a fire pit, with a 1:12 playworker-to-child ratio. Ship an insurer-approved risk-benefit policy, playworker training, a phone-locker rule and flexible memberships. Anchor demand with full-day Fridays in four-day-week districts, then add weekday afternoons and holiday camps.
why_now: More than 2,100 public schools in 26 states now run four-day weeks and the number is growing, mostly in rural districts with few child-care options. At the same time school phone bans and the 'anxious generation' movement have made parents ask for offline peer time.
revenue_model: Monthly memberships, per-day Friday fees (about $50 x 35-40 Fridays is roughly $2,000 per child per year), birthday parties, holiday camps, and later franchise or license fees.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce good is not activities, it is unsupervised-feeling time with peers, and what makes it sellable is liability engineering: an insurance-approved risk policy and playwork training that let a for-profit offer what municipalities avoid. Four-day weeks give a ready anchor customer (working parents with an empty Friday) that funds the more interesting weekday model.
first_30_days: Choose a four-day-week district with a supportive superintendent and rent a church hall or barn for about $1k/month. Hire two playworkers, secure a youth-program insurance policy, and pre-sell 25 Friday memberships through school newsletters and Facebook groups. Run four pilot Fridays, gather parent and kid feedback, then add after-school hours.

title: Real-Factory Credentials From Customs Shipping Records
one_liner: Turn public US import records into supplier-owned reputation credentials and audit-ready reasonable-care dossiers that prove a factory is a real manufacturer.
customer: Small and mid-size US importers of record (Amazon and Shopify brands, furniture, hardware and apparel distributors) re-sourcing to Vietnam, India, Mexico and Turkey. Customs brokers are a channel, and factories are the second payer.
problem: The importer of record is investigated first, and liability turns on whether it exercised reasonable care about the supplier's origin claims. In August 2026 the White House published a report on transshipment, a 40% penalty tariff applies, and CBP has expanded inspections of shipments from Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Mexico. Small importers cannot tell a real factory from a trading company or a re-labeller, and sourcing agents' claims are unverifiable.
solution: Supplier Proof. Build a profile per factory from three or more years of US import records (shipper and consignee names, volumes, product codes, ports, cadence) plus corporate registry and location data, flag anomalies such as volume beyond plausible capacity, mismatched product codes or shell-company addresses, and add optional local inspector visits. Factories claim and verify their profile and can consent to name repeat buyers as references. The output is a dossier the importer can hand to a broker or to CBP.
why_now: Tariff enforcement moved in 2025-26 from headline rates to origin verification, and the August 2026 transshipment report has put importer liability on every compliance officer's desk. Sourcing shifts away from China are happening now, so millions of dollars of orders are going to unfamiliar factories.
revenue_model: Importer subscriptions of $149-499 per month, $150-400 per dossier, inspector visits passed through at a margin, and $600-1,200 per year from factories for a verified credential once importers demand it.
non_obvious_insight: Import records are the only unforgeable cross-border reputation ledger for factories, but they are sold as raw rows to analysts. Repackaged as supplier-owned credentials with a reasonable-care wrapper, a data product becomes a compliance product with a real budget line: avoiding a 40% penalty.
first_30_days: Buy 12 months of import records for two categories (for example furniture and hardware from Vietnam and India). Auto-build about 1,000 factory profiles and hand-audit 20. Send 200 emails to sourcing managers and customs brokers. Sell the first 10 dossiers at $250 each and use them to refine the scoring.

title: Statutory Records-Portal Autopilot for Florida HOAs
one_liner: An email-in service that auto-posts a small Florida condo or HOA board's required documents to a compliant owner-only portal and tracks the deadlines.
customer: Self-managed Florida condo associations with 25+ units and HOAs with 100+ parcels, run by volunteer boards who cannot afford enterprise community-management software. The board treasurer or secretary pays, on the advice of the association's attorney or CPA.
problem: Florida law now requires these associations to post official records online. Condos of 25+ units must post the declaration and bylaws, minutes and meeting videos for the preceding 12 months, contracts and bid summaries over $500, budgets, financial reports, meeting notices and inspection reports and reserve studies, within 30 days of receiving or creating them (Fla. Stat. 718.111(12)(g)). HOAs with 100+ parcels had to post their equivalent documents behind an owner-only portal by January 1, 2025 (Fla. Stat. 720.303). Volunteer boards miss the posting clocks, and the resident-app market serves them poorly: a TownSq reviewer, a condo president, says the app gives 'no information that allows my board to manage our association effectively'. Others report that 'mailing settings were disabled... no one received mailed statements', a 2-page PDF shows only its first page, and requests cannot be edited after submission.
solution: Boards forward minutes, bids, contracts, budgets and inspection reports to a dedicated inbox, or drop meeting recordings into a folder. The system sorts each item into the statute's document categories and redacts protected information for board approval. It posts to an owner-only portal inside the 30-day clock and keeps meeting notices and agendas on their required schedule. It expires minutes and videos on a rolling 12-month cycle and keeps a compliance scorecard showing what is posted, what is missing and when each item is due. It also logs owner records requests with response deadlines.
why_now: The posting duties are in force: the HOA portal deadline was January 1, 2025, and the condo website provision is in the current statute. Florida has also been changing its condo and HOA rules, and attorneys are warning boards about compliance. A board that receives a records demand or a lawyer's letter will pay for a fix that week. The resident apps boards would otherwise use are rated poorly for board tasks.
revenue_model: $149-$299 per month per association depending on units, plus a $500 setup fee to load and classify the existing records. Referral fees to community-association attorneys and CPAs who recommend it. Add-ons: meeting-video hosting and a document translation for multilingual communities.
non_obvious_insight: The mandate creates a legal need in the segment with the least budget. Big vendors serve professionally managed communities, while the volunteer boards of small associations only need the documents posted correctly and on time. The statute itself says a failure to post 'is not in and of itself sufficient to invalidate any action or decision' of the board and specifies no fine, so the buyer is motivated by attorney advice, owner complaints and records-request risk, not by fines or features, and the pitch should reflect that. Evidence: the statute text at http://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0700-0799/0718/Sections/0718.111.html (condos) and http://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0700-0799/0720/Sections/0720.303.html (HOAs, Jan 1, 2025). Resident-app gaps from TownSq Community reviews (a condo president says it provides 'no information that allows my board to manage'; disabled mailed statements; a 2-page PDF shows only page 1) at https://itunes.apple.com/us/rss/customerreviews/id=945419466/sortby=mostrecent/xml. The pain is in board and owner communication, not the payments those apps focus on.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: build the inbox-to-portal flow for the 15 statutory document types and a redaction review screen. Have a Florida community-association attorney review the category list and the redaction rules. Days 10-20: run a free public compliance scan on 200 associations in Palm Beach, Broward and Miami-Dade using their public websites and email the board the gaps. Days 20-30: sign 2-3 community-association law firms as referral partners and take the first 10 associations at $199/month.

title: Plumber Doorstep Network for Lead Line Access
one_liner: Sell water utilities and their engineering consultants a local-plumber network that verifies unknown service-line materials, converts homeowner access agreements and does the interior tie-ins on lead and galvanized line replacements.
customer: Municipal and regional water utilities (10k-200k connections) with a large 'unknown material' share in their lead service line inventory, and the engineering consultants running their inventories and replacement programs, funded by state revolving funds and Bipartisan Infrastructure Law money.
problem: Utilities must identify every unknown-material service line and replace lead and galvanized-requiring-replacement lines, including the private side, under the federal Lead and Copper Rule Improvements; several states (Michigan, New Jersey, Illinois) have their own mandates. The bottleneck is not excavation, it is access. Mailer response rates are low, homeowner self-identification is unreliable, and people do not want a stranger from Public Works in the basement. The utility's excavation contractor also usually refuses to touch interior plumbing, so the interior reconnection sits in limbo. EPA's own August 2026 access-tips document exists because this is where programs stall.
solution: A branded 'Local Plumber Verification' visit. A licensed plumber or apprentice from a local shop knocks on a scheduled visit, checks the pipe where it enters the house (scratch and magnet test, the wiped-joint bulge, meter connection, photo protocol) in about 10 minutes, and uploads a GIS-ready record to the inventory. They get the access agreement signed on the spot, note obstructions (finished basement, boxed-in pipe, shutoff condition) and pre-scope the interior tie-in. A second product is the interior tie-in and shutoff replacement, done by the same shops as a subcontract to the utility's excavation contractor, with a warranty on the house side.
why_now: The federal rule's ten-year replacement clock, the compliance dates approaching in 2027, EPA's freshly updated access guidance, and billions in SRF and BIL money that has to be spent all converge. Utilities are now measured on unknown-line reduction, and consultants are looking for boots on the ground. Even if federal deadlines are softened, the state laws and the fact that unknown lines still have to be identified keep the demand.
revenue_model: $60-120 per verified line, $150-300 per signed access agreement (both paid by utility or consultant per unit), and a 15-20% margin on interior tie-in subcontracts ($400-1,500 each). The shop keeps most of the field labor and pays the network for lead flow, tooling, quality control and the reporting workflow.
non_obvious_insight: Homeowners trust the truck with a local plumber's name on it far more than a city letter, and the plumber can read a lead line faster than any model can read a mailer. The reason programs stall is that homeowners fear that letting anyone in means they will be found to have a problem and get a bill, and that the utility contractor will leave their basement half-connected. A plumber solves both, and plumbers are the only people who already have a license, insurance and an interior-work warranty.
first_30_days: Skip direct municipal procurement at first and sell to a mid-size engineering consultant who already holds the utility's inventory contract and needs subcontractors. Pick two utilities with a high unknown share and low mailer response. Propose a paid pilot of 300 addresses at a fixed price per verification. Recruit 3 shops that want steady work for apprentices. Build the mobile form and photo protocol in a form tool that exports to the utility's inventory template.

title: Retreat Options for Eroding Oceanfront Homes
one_liner: An annual retainer that reserves a house-mover and demolition slot and triggers automatically when satellite-measured setback hits a preset distance.
customer: Owners of oceanfront and bluff homes on the Outer Banks and Cape Hatteras, Great Lakes bluffs, Maine and Nantucket, and California bluffs. Secondary buyers are lenders, county governments and the National Park Service.
problem: 32 oceanfront houses have collapsed along Cape Hatteras National Seashore since 2020, four in one February 2026 weekend. Owners bear removal costs of roughly $120K to demolish or $100K-$200K to move. NFIP pays nothing pre-collapse, and contractor capacity is overwhelmed exactly when it is needed. NFIP pre-collapse coverage has been proposed but not enacted.
solution: Pooled owners pay a retainer for two things. First, monthly satellite measurement of foundation-to-scarp or vegetation-line distance from 30-50 cm imagery, with pre-storm tasking, and archive imagery to compute each home's 5-10 year retreat rate. Second, pre-negotiated capacity with movers and demolition contractors. Preset thresholds automatically mobilise the contractor and deliver a dated evidence file. That file doubles as claim documentation if NFIP pre-collapse legislation passes and gives lenders and counties a trusted trigger. Structured as a service and capacity contract rather than insurance.
why_now: FEMA's lack of any pre-collapse option is national news in September 2026 (NPR), and the Outer Banks lost 20 Buxton houses in a year. Pre-collapse coverage legislation is pending. Cheap oversupplied commercial imagery makes pooled tasking affordable (one 25 km2 pass covers about 10 km of coast and hundreds of homes).
revenue_model: $1,800/yr retainer per home. An 8-10% referral fee on move or demolition jobs. County and NPS triage contracts. Lender monitoring feeds at $10-20 per loan per month.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource is neither money nor measurement but contractor capacity at the moment of crisis. An option on that capacity, triggered by a measurement all parties trust, is a new kind of asset. Neighbours pooling their tasking makes the satellite cost trivial per home.
first_30_days: Sign 2 Outer Banks or Great Lakes house-movers and demolition firms to retainer terms. Pull archive imagery to compute 5-year retreat rates for about 200 threatened homes, then approach owner associations in Buxton and Rodanthe with each home's own curve. Enrol 10 homes at $1,200 founder pricing.

title: CPAP Off-Ramp: Retire Machines, Refurbish for Uninsured
angle: Pairing 1: GLP-1/preventive medicine x Device reuse and refurbishment
one_liner: Re-test sleep apnea at each weight-loss milestone, help patients who have gone into remission safely come off CPAP, and refurbish the retired machines for the newly uninsured.
customer: Medicare Advantage plans and self-insured employers (paying a share of avoided rental and supply costs), cash-pay GLP-1 patients paying for the recheck, and safety-net clinics buying refurbished units.
problem: Tirzepatide is approved for moderate-to-severe OSA in adults with obesity, and in SURMOUNT-OSA 43% to 52% of patients at the top dose met disease-resolution criteria, with apnea-hypopnea events cut by up to about 60%. Nobody is paid to notice. DME suppliers earn on continued mask and hose resupply, sleep labs earn on tests, and patients keep machines in the closet. After 13 months of Medicare rental the patient owns the machine, so it can simply be donated. Meanwhile about 4.8M people are newly uninsured after the ACA subsidy expiry, with millions more Medicaid losses due in 2027, and a $800-1,000 CPAP is out of reach.
solution: A physician-supervised pathway with a disposable home sleep apnea test at each 10% weight-loss milestone and a telehealth sleep-physician review. Patients who qualify taper or stop PAP, and are offered a buy-back credit or donation. Returned machines are sanitized, function-tested, data-wiped and re-kitted with new humidifier chambers, filters and tubing, then re-issued via licensed DME partners and clinics at roughly $150-250. Motors, foam and plastics from units that fail go to recycling.
why_now: Zepbound's OSA indication is now established and Part D can cover it. The cash-pay pill wave and the July 2026 Medicare Bridge bring far more patients on-drug. ACA and Medicaid losses create a cash-pay buyer base for cheap devices.
revenue_model: Performance fee from payers or employers of about 30% of first-year avoided rental and supply cost. Cash-pay recheck ($79-129). Margin on refurbished device sales, with a nonprofit partner able to receive donation tax deductions.
non_obvious_insight: GLP-1 success silently strands both a recurring billing stream and a physical asset. The party that finds the stranded machine can be paid twice: once by the payer for the avoided spend and once by the uninsured buyer for the second life.
first_30_days: Contract a tele-sleep physician group and a licensed DME partner. Recruit 100 patients from a cash-pay telehealth partner who have OSA and are on tirzepatide. Write the refurbishment SOP against manufacturer cleaning guidance and state DME rules. Sell the first payer or employer pilot on a savings-share basis with retrospective claims data.

title: Responsible-Charge Network for AI-Made Professional Work
one_liner: Licensed engineers and architects take legal responsibility for AI-generated permit sets per review, with a review-telemetry audit trail that also lowers malpractice premiums.
customer: AI-native firms that generate permit drawings, structural letters and MEP plans for ADUs, solar, decks and prefab, and the small design firms that use them. They need licensed sign-off in many states and don't want to employ engineers everywhere.
problem: AI can draft a permit set in an hour, but only a licensed human can seal it. Startups hire engineers state by state or rely on stamp mills. Regulators and insurers fear rubber-stamping, and 'responsible charge' (the legal standard that the professional actually directed the work) is unprovable. Existing AI-drawing companies such as Spacial keep licensed engineers in-house, so smaller entrants have no good option.
solution: A vetted network of licensed professionals paid a fixed fee per stamped package, plus software that records how the review happened: time on sheet, checks completed, redlines, overrides. That log becomes the defensible 'responsible-charge' record for state boards, and it underwrites cheaper E&O coverage through an MGA partner. Start narrow with structural and engineering letters for residential ADU, deck and solar permits in three states.
why_now: AI permit-set generators are moving from demos to real volume, and the standard practice is a licensed engineer reviewing before sealing. Professional liability carriers now ask about AI use, and licensing boards are issuing AI guidance. Nobody has built the shared review-evidence layer.
revenue_model: 25% to 35% take on engineer fees of $150 to $600 per package. MGA commission on E&O premiums. SaaS fee for the telemetry and audit-trail software.
non_obvious_insight: In AI-delivered professional services, the scarce input is not intelligence but a person who can lose a license. Whoever holds verifiable proof of actual review owns the pricing of liability, which is worth more than the stamps. The product is explicitly anti-stamp-mill: it makes shallow review visible and expensive.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 semi-retired PEs across three states. Sign two AI-permit startups or ADU designers with a backlog. Run the review flow manually with screen recordings and checklists to gather telemetry. Meet one small-firm E&O broker about a pilot rider for reviewed AI work.

title: Virtual Detention Basin from Smart Cisterns
one_liner: Thousands of backyard tanks that pre-drain before forecast storms, coordinated like a virtual power plant for stormwater.
customer: Stormwater utilities and sewer districts under combined-sewer consent decrees, and cities running basement-flooding programs.
problem: Utilities spend billions on tunnels and tanks to control overflows and basement flooding, while private-lot storage sits unmanaged because each barrel is dumb. FEMA money is unstable, so cities want cheaper capacity.
solution: Forecast-controlled cisterns and rain gardens with low-cost cellular valves that pre-drain ahead of storms and hold water at the peak, driven by AI weather ensemble forecasts. The utility pays per managed gallon at peak. First product is a 200-tank pilot in one sewershed, retrofitting existing barrels with a roughly $150 controller.
why_now: AI weather ensembles (operational since 2025) make per-storm control affordable, cellular valves are cheap, and consent-decree deadlines and unstable FEMA funding push cities toward distributed capacity.
revenue_model: Per managed gallon or per tank-year utility contracts, plus grants and rebates covering hardware.
non_obvious_insight: A city's cheapest new detention basin is 10,000 backyards coordinated like a virtual power plant.
first_30_days: Identify 3 combined-sewer cities with rebate programs, retrofit 50 existing barrels with controllers, and measure peak outflow reduction.

title: Blended-Beef Extender for Grinders and Schools
one_liner: Sell a fiber-and-protein extender that stretches ground beef 20-30% and adds fiber, instead of trying to replace beef.
customer: Regional ground-beef grinders, further processors, and school and institutional foodservice distributors.
problem: Retail beef hit a record $9.64/lb with the smallest herd in 75 years, and Mexican feeder cattle are halted. Plant-based meat failed as a replacement, so buyers have no cost-relief tool.
solution: A mushroom, legume and oat fiber-protein blend with a clean label, tested in 70/30 and 80/20 beef blends, sold by the ton with USDA-compliant blended-product labeling and recipe support.
why_now: Record beef prices, screwworm-driven supply risk, and GLP-1 users who want more protein and fiber per bite make a cheaper high-fiber blended patty newly attractive.
revenue_model: Ingredient sales per pound, co-development fees, and multi-year supply agreements with distributors.
non_obvious_insight: Plant-based meat lost as an identity swap but wins as a cost and fiber additive inside real beef, where the buyer never has to change what they say they are selling.
first_30_days: Contract a food-science lab to build three blends, send samples to about 10 regional grinders and two school-food distributors, and start FSIS labeling work.

title: H-2A Housing-as-a-Service for Growers
one_liner: Lease pre-certified modular seasonal housing by the bed so growers can actually use H-2A visas.
customer: Specialty-crop growers and farm labor contractors in CA, WA, GA and the Southeast.
problem: Immigration enforcement removed at least 155,000 farm workers and H-2A is projected to grow toward 500k jobs, but employers must supply inspected housing, which is scarce and slow to build.
solution: A fleet of modular bunk units that pass DOL and OSHA housing inspection, delivered to farms or leased sites for the season, with paperwork and maintenance handled.
why_now: The October 2025 wage-rule change and enforcement-driven crew losses push growers to H-2A at scale, making beds the binding constraint.
revenue_model: Per-bed-month lease of roughly $X seasonal contracts with multi-year renewals.
non_obvious_insight: Visa wages get the headlines, but whoever owns compliant beds owns the labor channel. Housing is asset-backed, financeable and repeats every season.
first_30_days: Pre-sell 100 beds for the 2027 season to five growers with deposits, source used modular units, and get one prototype unit through a state housing inspection.

title: Lender-Required Benefit Records for F&I Add-Ons
one_liner: A 20-second, VIN-aware 'did this product actually benefit this buyer' check and signed record that indirect lenders demand as a funding stip, because California's CARS Act (SB 766) bans add-ons that provide no benefit and lenders inherit the exposure.
customer: Primary payer: credit unions and banks that buy indirect auto paper in California (dealer-management and compliance teams). Secondary: California franchised and independent dealer groups, at about $149 per store per month, when a lender tells them to use it.
problem: SB 766 becomes operative Oct 1, 2026. It bars charging for an add-on the buyer would not benefit from, requires clear disclosure that add-ons are optional, and requires dealers to keep records for two years. Lenders that buy the contracts carry Holder Rule and Rees-Levering exposure for what happens in the F&I office. Nobody outside the dealership can see whether GAP was sold to a buyer with 35% down, a 7-year service contract to a buyer with 6 years of factory powertrain warranty left, or prepaid oil changes to an EV buyer. The FTC's federal CARS Rule was vacated in January 2025, so states and private plaintiffs are the enforcement, and the April 2026 $78.1M Lindsay Automotive settlement shows the size of the downside.
solution: A lightweight web form and API that the F&I manager fills in per product during the menu. It auto-decodes the VIN (EV or hybrid, remaining factory warranty, tire type, key type). It pulls loan-to-value from the deal numbers and runs benefit rules per product, such as GAP with LTV under about 90%, a service contract that overlaps the factory warranty, maintenance on an EV, and key replacement on a keyless-start car. It flags mismatches, captures a one-tap 'customer chose this anyway, here's why' rationale, and outputs a timestamped PDF and JSON record. Lenders add it to their funding-package checklist. The rule library is the product and is updated per state as CARS-style bills spread.
why_now: SB 766 takes effect in three days (Oct 1, 2026). Federal rule-making is dead, so the compliance burden has moved to states and to lenders' third-party-risk teams. More states are copying California's language. The Lindsay $78.1M settlement in April 2026 made every dealer compliance director and every credit union counsel pay attention.
revenue_model: Per-funded-contract fee of $2 to $4 paid by the lender or passed to the dealer, or a $149 per store per month dealer subscription. Later, sell state-by-state rule packs and an anonymized benefit-mismatch benchmark to lenders and dealer insurers.
non_obvious_insight: Most dealer violations are not lies. They are menu autopilot. The DMS menu shows the same five products on every deal and the pay plan rewards penetration, so a mismatch happens without anyone deciding to deceive. The buyer who will pay for compliance is not the dealer, whose incentive is to sell. It is the lender, who holds the paper, gets sued alongside the dealer, and has the leverage to make a data field mandatory at funding.
first_30_days: Read the SB 766 text and the FTC's vacated rule for the exact 'no benefit' examples, and turn them into 25 to 30 explicit rules. Build a plain web form with no DMS integration. Cold-pitch compliance officers at 15 California credit unions with big indirect books through the CUNA/California credit union compliance channels. Offer a free 60-day pilot in which they require it from their 3 to 5 highest-volume dealers. Pre-sell 10 dealers at $99 per month using the line 'your lender is going to ask for this.'

title: Flight Recorder for AI-Drafted Police Reports
angle: Pairing 2: Creator economy & media provenance x Government/public sector/defense/municipal services (process-based authorship proof x municipal policing)
one_liner: Vendor-agnostic middleware that captures the AI draft, every officer edit and timestamp, then issues a court-ready authorship record, the process-based 'human-made' proof creators lack, so prosecutors will accept AI-assisted reports.
customer: Police departments and sheriffs' offices ($60-150 per officer per year), city and county attorneys and DA offices that must vouch for reports, and public defender offices (per-case discovery audits).
problem: Tools such as Axon's Draft One write narratives from body-cam audio, and reporting in 2025 said original AI drafts are not retained (prior knowledge). California SB 524 (effective 2026) requires disclosure of AI use and retention of first drafts, Utah requires disclaimers, and King County prosecutors said in 2024 they would reject AI-assisted reports (prior knowledge). Defense has the same failure mode: a SOCOM analyst's chatbot fabricated a ship's cargo manifest that was formatted as an official intelligence summary, with no provenance layer in the workflow.
solution: A capture layer inside the report editor or records-management system logs the body-cam transcript hash, the AI draft, each officer edit as a diff, and time-on-task, with per-paragraph officer attestations ('I observed' or 'I reviewed'). It emits a signed content-credential-style record attached to the report, a redacted discovery packet for defense, and a DA-portal view that applies each office's acceptance rules.
why_now: State laws requiring disclosure and draft retention are in force in 2026. AI report-writing is spreading while DA acceptance remains the gate. Process-based provenance standards (C2PA) now exist, and GenAI.mil's 2M-user rollout shows the same official-looking-AI-text problem is arriving federally.
revenue_model: Per-officer SaaS, per-case discovery-packet fees to public defenders, and later federal licenses for labeling AI-assisted analytic products.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck to AI report-writing is admissibility and credibility, not accuracy, and the real gatekeepers are DAs, not police chiefs. A DA who publishes an acceptance standard requiring a verifiable authorship record forces every vendor to comply, so give the standard to DAs first and sell the ledger to departments second.
first_30_days: Get one DA's office in a state with an SB 524-style law to co-draft an acceptance standard. Prototype a Word and Google Docs add-in plus a records-system-neutral upload, pilot it with 2 small departments already testing AI report tools, and offer public defenders an 'AI-report discovery audit' service.
